description:
Pothos (Epipremnum aureum), also known as Devil's Ivy, is a very common houseplant with long, trailing vines. It is not safe for cats, especially since its hanging leaves are often tempting for curious pets to play with and chew.

The main danger comes from tiny, sharp needles inside the plant's cells called insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. When a cat bites into the leaves or stems, these microscopic needles shoot out and stab the tissues of the mouth, tongue, and throat. This causes sudden and sharp pain rather than a body-wide illness. Because the pain happens right away, most cats stop chewing before they eat a large amount.

If a cat bites a pothos plant, they may start drooling heavily, paw at their mouth in pain, or vomit. You might also see swelling around their lips, mouth, and tongue. In severe cases, the swelling can make it hard for the cat to swallow. Move trailing vines completely out of reach, and contact a veterinarian if the swelling is bad or if your cat has trouble swallowing.
name: Pothos / Devil’s Ivy
safetyNotes: Main hazard: Insoluble calcium oxalate raphides in the leaves and stems irritate the mouth and throat when chewed.
Symptoms: Sudden mouth pain, heavy drooling, pawing at the mouth, swollen lips or tongue, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing.
Access risk: Trailing vines are easy for cats to reach when they hang over shelves, tables, or plant stands.
Action: Move the plant out of reach, offer water or gently rinse the mouth if safe, and contact a vet if swelling or swallowing trouble appears.

symptoms.name: Intense burning, irritation, and pain of the mouth, lips, and tongue
Swelling of the mouth and tongue, accompanied by difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
